intro:
Use it for a message that belongs to a page and stays there until it has been dealt with: a payment that failed, a limit that is close, a form that needs another look.

By default the message is a card set into a tray tinted in its `tone`, and `Alert.Actions` sit in the strip of tray under the card, at its end. `variant="plain"` is one tinted box, for inside a form or a dialog that already has an edge. `variant="banner"` is one line across the top of a page or a panel.

An alert does not leave on its own. It stays until `Alert.Close` is pressed or `open` is set to false, and then it folds away.
usage:
<Alert tone="warning">
  <Alert.Icon />
  <Alert.Title>Storage is 90% full</Alert.Title>
  <Alert.Description>Uploads stop at 50 GB.</Alert.Description>
  <Alert.Actions>
    <Button size="sm">Upgrade</Button>
  </Alert.Actions>
  <Alert.Close />
</Alert>

parts.Icon: The glyph at the start, in the tone's colour. In the default variant it sits in a disc of that colour. Without children it draws the tone's own glyph.
parts.Title: What happened, in a few words.
parts.Description: The sentence under the title. A link in it is underlined.
parts.Details: A line under the description that opens into a list, for an alert that sums up several things. `label` is the line's text.
parts.Item: One entry in the list, marked with a dot in the tone's colour.
parts.Actions: The buttons. In the default variant they move out of the card into the tray under it; in `plain` they sit under the words, and in `banner` at the end of the line. Keep it a direct child of `Alert`.
parts.Close: A round cross at the end that folds the alert away. It calls `onOpenChange(false)`.

examples.title: Tones
examples.description: `tone` draws the alert in one of the theme's roles: `neutral`, `info`, `success`, `warning` or `destructive`. The tray takes a little of the colour and the icon's disc a little more; the words stay in the foreground colours, so they read the same in every tone.

examples.title: With actions
examples.description: `Alert.Actions` sits in the tray under the card, at its end, so the buttons do not crowd the sentence they answer. `Alert.Icon` takes any glyph as its children.

examples.title: Dismissing
examples.description: `Alert.Close` folds the alert to no height, and what is under it slides up. Here `open` is held outside, so a button can bring it back.

examples.title: A list of problems
examples.description: `Alert.Details` adds a line under the description that opens into a list of `Alert.Item`s. The title gives the count; the list names each one.

examples.title: Plain
examples.description: `variant="plain"` is one tinted box with the glyph alone, for a note under a field or a warning inside a panel. Its actions sit under the words.

examples.title: Banner
examples.description: `variant="banner"` is one line across the top of what it is about, with square ends and a rule under it. Keep it to a title and one action: the line is read at a glance, and a sentence beside the title crowds it. On a narrow screen the action wraps under the title.

notes:
### Tone and screen readers

A `destructive` or `warning` alert has `role="alert"`, so a screen reader announces it as soon as it appears. The other tones have `role="status"` and are read when the reader reaches them. Pass `role` to choose for yourself.

### Closing

A closed alert stays in the page at no height, and nothing inside it can be focused. Use `open` and `onOpenChange` to hold the state outside, for example to remember that it was dismissed. In a column with a `gap`, the gap stays where the alert was.

### Actions in the tray

The default variant finds `Alert.Actions` among its own children and moves it into the tray, so keep it a direct child rather than wrapping it in another component.
